ai.claude: Reporting by headquarters is a common, legal method, so the change alone proves nothing. But together with the WSJ findings it points to the real weakness of export controls: they track who pays, not where the chip runs. After Jensen Huang's exit, Nvidia's next filing will be read closely for any change in how China exposure is disclosed.
ai.fact: The Wall Street Journal reported this weekend that large data centres in Southeast Asia gave Chinese companies access to Nvidia computing power through a gap in US sanctions, and served as cover for alleged chip smuggling. Michael Burry notes that in late 2025 Nvidia switched from counting revenue by billing location to counting it by customer headquarters, after which Singapore's fast-growing share stopped showing in the figures.

opinion.text: argues the change made it harder to see where Nvidia's chips really end up, says the press has finally started to scrutinise the company, and says he still holds put options on the stock.

austrian.claude: The arithmetic is the Treasury's own, but the conclusion is not automatic. Fed independence is still real: it hiked in September against the Treasury's wishes, and 10-year yields above 5% show markets demanding more, not less, from the Fed. Higher taxes or growth from AI could also narrow the gap, even if neither looks likely soon.
austrian.fact: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Friday that the Fed should not hike too much into an energy supply shock and that core inflation remains under control. The Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023. The Treasury's own Financial Report projects federal debt held by the public rising from 99% of GDP to over 150% by 2040, and Social Security's trustees expect its retirement trust fund to run dry in late 2032.

opinion.text: calls this fiscal dominance in the open: with $12 trillion to refinance by the end of next year and $103 billion of interest paid in October alone, Washington will borrow rather than cut, and the Fed will end up printing to buy the debt.

mainstream.fact: SRF reports that the popular vote on the Bilaterals III package with the EU will most likely come in 2028 at the earliest, because the Council of States has not yet scheduled the reconciliation of differences with the National Council. The package, which updates market access, wages protection and Switzerland's contribution to the EU, has split parties for two years.
